title: Apple, AMD, Palantir Lead Big Earnings Week

The discussion is mostly technical chart commentary (buy zones, moving-average levels, relative strength) paired with consensus EPS and revenue expectations and year-over-year growth figures. Hosts make no explicit guaranteed-return claims, but they lean on chart-pattern language and repeatedly say a stock is "extended" or wait for a buy point. No position disclosure was given.

title: The Bulls Are Trapped | TCAF 266

He argues the market is tactically bearish for the next several weeks, citing a quant timing model, crowded positioning, heavy equity issuance, and tighter credit spreads for AI data-center debt, while noting the hyperscalers have so far been resilient. The episode also includes off-topic banter about Manhattan neighborhoods and the host's nickname.

US household equity ownership and the share of household net worth in stocks are described as at or near record highs, with 401k inflows described as a steady buying source.
Retail and passive/systematic flows are described as a volatility dampener, and the speaker argues the stock market now drives the economy via the wealth effect.
AI capex is described as consuming a large share of hyperscaler revenue, with the speaker questioning how the spending will be covered by revenue.
Index-level correlation among S&P 500 stocks is described as unusually low, with relative-value and multi-manager pod crowding cited as a cause.

Management said the US PrEP market grew 14% year-over-year in the quarter.

findings.summary: This is a transcript of Eli Lilly's Q3 2026 earnings call (the video is a Benzinga stream of the call). Management reported strong Q3 growth (revenue up about 39%, driven by Mounjaro, Zepbound and international growth), raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $91-92B and non-GAAP EPS guidance to $35-36, and walked through pipeline updates (retatrutide and orforglipron trial data, FDA approvals, acquisitions) and Q&A on Medicare GLP-1 bridge uptake, pricing, and M&A. Management also noted about $2B of one-time items in 2026 revenue that it does not expect to recur, and said 2027 guidance will come in January.
macro_points: Management described the obesity category as the largest new category expansion in pharmaceutical history, with penetration still low (roughly 1 in 10 eligible US patients reached, per management).

Medicare GLP-1 bridge program cited by management as having over half a million prescriptions filled since July 1 and a USC study estimating over $20B in 10-year Medicare savings from anti-obesity medication expansion (the study is cited by management, not independently verified in the call).
Management expects commercial access to remain relatively stable through 2027, with Medicare and Medicaid coverage growth shifting mix toward lower net price.
red_flags: Revenue benefited by roughly $900M in Q3 and about $2B for the year from one-time items (milestones and rebate/discount estimate changes), which management says will not recur; underlying growth is less than headline figures suggest.
US price declined about 7% in Q3 (about 10% excluding a favorable adjustment), and management expects net price to remain a headwind in 2027.

Early-stage pipeline data (retatrutide, orforglipron, the triple agonist bimagrutide/Allora TZP phase 2) are company-reported topline results; management acknowledged higher discontinuation rates at the highest dose of the triple agonist.
Medicare bridge program is a pilot; its continuation beyond 2027 is not assured and management said it will be discussed with CMS later.
Management acknowledged past guidance has been conservative and that the company is largely projecting in uncharted territory, so forecasting uncertainty is high.
Heavy reliance on the obesity/incretin franchise (roughly $16B quarterly revenue) for growth.

tickers.thesis: Management presented Q3 results as strong and raised 2026 guidance by roughly $10B on revenue, citing better-than-expected Medicare bridge uptake and international Mounjaro growth. It framed the incretin market as early in penetration with a long runway and pointed to a broad late-stage pipeline in obesity, oncology, immunology and neuroscience.
tickers.timeframe: 2026 full year; 2027 guidance in January; Innovation Day December 7

title: SanDisk Q1 FY27 Earnings Call | $SNDK | 🔴 WATCH LIVE

findings.summary: This is a SanDisk fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call (Q&A portion included in transcript). Management reported revenue of about $11B (up 23% sequentially, well above guidance), non-GAAP gross margin of 85.1%, non-GAAP EPS of $49.51, $5.7B adjusted free cash flow, and $5B in buybacks. They guided fiscal Q2 revenue to $12.2–12.6B, EPS to $55–57 pre-split (announced 8-for-1 split), and repeated a strong AI-driven NAND demand thesis, long-term supply agreements ("NBMs"), and HBF product development timelines.
macro_points: Management expects a strong NAND market in calendar 2027, with data center around 55% of the market and bit demand growing about 40% year over year.
Management says PC and smartphone exabyte demand should grow in 2027 despite slightly lower unit counts, due to rising content per device.
Data center has grown from about 20% of industry bits early in the decade to roughly half today, per management's estimate.
Management expects KV cache to be about one-third of AI data center flash demand by decade end.
red_flags: Company-reported results and guidance are management's own claims; this is a company earnings call, not independent analysis.
Forward claims about AI-driven demand, NBM pipeline strength, and KV cache market share are asserted without independent data; the company declined to give specific share or bit-supply targets.
Management repeatedly said HBF is not in the long-term financial model and that its market opportunity is still undefined.
Consumer revenue fell 29% sequentially, and management did not give a Q3 guide, advising conservative sequential modeling because fiscal Q3 is seasonally weakest.
Large share of demand is tied to long-term customer commitments (NBMs), which management presents as visibility but whose terms and deposits were only partly described.

tickers.thesis: Management argues AI inference is structurally increasing NAND demand, with data center demand, long-term NBM customer agreements, and new products (BiCS 9/10, QLC, HBF) supporting growing, durable free cash flow and continued buybacks of excess cash. Supporting evidence is company-reported results and forward commentary, with growth attributed to both volume and pricing.
tickers.timeframe: next several quarters; NBM visibility through 2030
tickers.catalyst: 11/19 distribution of stock split shares; trading split-adjusted from 11/20; fiscal Q2 results guided at $12.2–12.6B revenue

title: Intel earnings show the company is 'still PC dependent', says Benchmark's Cody Acree

findings.summary: CNBC interview with Benchmark analyst Cody Acree after Intel's quarterly report and weak next-quarter guidance, with shares reported down about 22% in the aftermarket. Acree attributes the miss mainly to PC weakness, as OEMs returned to market-rate memory pricing after depleting cheaper inventory, and estimates the overall PC market could fall 20-25% this year. He says the data center (CPU/agentic AI) and foundry businesses were ahead of estimates and that Intel's long-term case rests on AI CPU demand and its foundry turnaround. He also discusses read-through to AMD, Micron and Seagate.
macro_points: Estimates for the overall PC market are down 20-25% this year, per the host's cited estimates.
PC lifecycles have been extending into three-to-five-year periods, and CFOs may delay purchases amid uncertain memory prices.
Memory supply-demand dynamics expected to be similarly tight next year, so cheaper PCs are unlikely soon.
Shift toward agentic AI inference is expected to increase reliance on CPUs.
red_flags: Stock move (about 22% drop) is cited without price targets or valuation discussion.
Analyst's claims about the data center and foundry beats and the 'real TSMC competitor' thesis are asserted without specific figures in the transcript.
Transcript is auto-generated and some figures are garbled (e.g., the foundry beat amount and EPS number), so exact numbers are uncertain.
No discussion of downside risk to the bull thesis beyond the PC weakness.

tickers.thesis: Acree says the quarter's miss and weak guidance are driven by PC demand, which he calls a cyclical downdraft, while data center CPU demand from agentic AI and foundry progress (14A engagement) remain the reasons to own the stock. He says the AI CPU and foundry story is intact despite the near-term miss.
tickers.catalyst: Quarterly earnings and fourth-quarter guidance miss

tickers.thesis: Acree says AMD is also PC-dependent but has more enterprise exposure and AI accelerator shipments, making it somewhat more defensible than Intel; AMD reports next week.

red_flags: Segment is short and largely political commentary; no investment analysis or market data is provided, so it offers no basis for trading decisions.

title: BofA’s Cabana Asks Fed on Rate Hikes ‘Why Wait Now?’

findings.summary: Bank of America strategist Mark Cabana discusses the Federal Reserve's posture ahead of an October FOMC meeting. He argues inflation is broadening in CPI and PPI while the Fed signals patience, which he finds confusing and speculates could be political or coordinated among Fed leadership. He says the bond market is currently calm enough to let the Fed hold, but that a rise in long-end yields could force a hike. The discussion is macro/rates commentary about Fed policy, not a stock recommendation.
macro_points: Inflation appears to be broadening in CPI and PPI, possibly from diesel prices spilling over and owners' equivalent rent bottoming.
The Fed is guiding toward a patient, quarterly hiking cadence before the data arrives, which the host finds inconsistent with the data.

Long-end Treasury yields are calm, which the host reads as the market accepting a Fed hold for now, partly due to risk-asset wobbles, tech-name questions, and European political stress (France, Italy).
Host speculates Fed leadership (Warsh, Williams, Jefferson) may be coordinating guidance, and that political pressure is possible, though he says he has no evidence.
red_flags: Speculation about political motivation of Fed officials with no supporting evidence, acknowledged by the speaker as speculation.
Forecast that the bond market will force a Fed hike is hedged ('not guaranteeing') but still a directional call on an unpredictable event.

title: United ‘Still Solidly Profitable’ as Fuels Costs Rise, CEO Kirby Says

findings.summary: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, interviewed at the company's Houston terminal, says the airline is still solidly profitable despite higher fuel costs, though second-half earnings are below last year's and below prior expectations. He says United has passed roughly 72% of the fuel increase to customers, that fare increases lag fuel costs, and that booking yields are up 20%+ recently, so full recapture is expected later rather than by year end. Most of the interview then covers Kirby's comments on a wealth tax and the backlash they drew, which are not investment analysis.
macro_points: Jet fuel prices have risen sharply this year from pandemic lows, though still below pre-COVID levels in real terms, per the CEO.
Airfares are rising but the CEO says they are still low in real terms versus pre-COVID; consumer demand described as resilient with load factors down about half a point in the quarter.
Premium cabin demand strong; CEO says economy demand has grown faster in recent quarters.
red_flags: Company-sourced management commentary with no independent verification of the 72% pass-through or yield figures.
Management expects full fuel cost recapture only after a lag, and says second-half earnings are below prior-year and expectations; the outlook is uncertain and dependent on fuel prices.
Interview pivots substantially to non-financial political commentary (wealth tax) that is unrelated to the investment case.

tickers.thesis: CEO says the airline is still solidly profitable despite fuel costs, that fares are rising with a lag and booking yields are up 20%+, and that it expects to recover most or all of the fuel increase over time. Also points to premium product investments (Starlink, seatback entertainment, app) as differentiators.
tickers.catalyst: Fuel price trajectory; pricing recapture in the coming quarters; next earnings

title: United CEO Kirby on Why he supports a wealth tax

findings.summary: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, interviewed by Bloomberg Television, explains his comment in a New York Times interview that he supports taxing wealth growth, which he framed as a fairness issue and a "nonconsensus opinion" rather than policy advocacy. He argues passive investment growth goes untaxed while wages face income tax, and suggests a wealth tax or similar approach paired with lower income taxes. The interview also covers backlash (including a governor's criticism and a public boycott pledge), and he floats national service as an idea for bringing the country together. No company or stock is discussed, so this is not a market-analysis piece.
macro_points: Wealth tax on investment growth, paired with lower income taxes, is framed as fairer than current treatment of passive income.
Wealth inequality and a 'K-shaped' economy are referenced as background.
National service (military, teaching, firefighting) floated as a unifying policy idea.
Long-term fiscal concerns cited: federal deficits and Social Security.
red_flags: Host and guest both note the remarks are a personal opinion, not a formal policy position, so the claims are not a substantiated policy analysis.
No figures are offered to support the claim that wealth growth goes untaxed in a way that is unfair, or to estimate revenue from a wealth tax.
Not investment content: no ticker, price, or trading view is expressed, so no market-related promotion is present.

title: Coke's Struggle to Break Into the $500 Billion Global Coffee Market
Bose CEO Lila Snyder on Skullcandy Acquisition

findings.summary: An interview with Bose CEO Lila Snyder about Bose's acquisition of Skullcandy, which followed a licensing partnership of a couple of years. She described Skullcandy as a growth acquisition aimed at a younger, active-lifestyle customer base within a multi-brand portfolio alongside McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Bose. She declined to disclose the price or whether it was paid in cash, and discussed supply chain, holiday demand, new wired headphones, and edge AI. The interview is company-management commentary with no investment recommendation.
macro_points: Consumers are feeling financial constraints, but audio is a passion category where spending tends to hold up, per the CEO.
Memory component costs are a pricing challenge; the company says it is trying to hold prices steady into the holiday season.
Supply chain is a focus; the CEO says the company has become more agile and resilient over the last 4-5 years.
red_flags: Acquisition price and payment form (cash vs. other) undisclosed, so the deal's value cannot be assessed.
No financial figures on Skullcandy's revenue, growth, or profitability were given; 'growth acquisition' claim is unsupported by data.
Interviewer cited a roughly $200 million take-private valuation about a decade ago, but the CEO did not confirm or give a current value.
Company-side interview: management statements about strategy and demand are not independently verified.

title: Musk needs 50% of Tesla's shares, and he cannot be in the room | The 8:30

findings.summary: Hosts discuss Elon Musk's comments that SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a possible merger at shareholder request. Musk said he is conflicted and won't join those discussions, that he thinks a merger would be a good idea, and that Tesla shareholders would ultimately vote, with a 50% approval bar. The hosts then focus on SpaceX's AI/data center spending plans (targets of 10-20 GW, roughly $40-50B per GW cited by hosts, about $19.6B spent last quarter) and Musk's claim that SpaceX could exit 2027 at $500B-$1T annualized revenue, which they say is a hard target that some analysts doubt.
red_flags: Merger is speculative: hosts note it is not a certainty and the deal would face regulatory scrutiny and shareholder votes
Forward revenue target ($500B-$1T annualized by end of 2027) is aggressive and hosts say some people disagree; it is an annualized run-rate, not collected revenue
Large capital needs (multi-billion dollars per gigawatt) with hosts saying the cash is not yet on hand, implying future debt or equity raises
Hosts' per-gigawatt cost figures are inconsistent with each other in the transcript and are unsourced estimates
macro_points: Possible SpaceX-Tesla merger would be among the largest corporate mergers in history and would likely face regulatory scrutiny from Washington
AI data center buildout requires very large capital spending across the industry

tickers.thesis: Hosts discuss a possible merger with SpaceX that would require Tesla shareholder approval, and raise concerns that Musk's control over a combined entity would be large. No clear buy or sell view is given on Tesla itself.
tickers.catalyst: Possible SpaceX merger and shareholder vote; no timeline given

tickers.thesis: Hosts describe SpaceX's large AI/data center buildout and reported AI revenue growth of about 830% year over year to roughly $7.6B, but say it has large funding needs and that its stated targets are very ambitious. One cited analyst (Gokul Hariharan at Evercore, described as bullish) says SpaceX still has much to prove, especially on compute build, monetization, and funding, but believes it has pricing leverage.
tickers.catalyst: Path to 10-20 GW power capacity, 2027 revenue target, and funding raises

Hosts gave no explicit financial position or valuation view on any stock discussed
macro_points: Mortgage rates eased slightly (30-year fixed at about 6.41% from 6.5%), but mortgage purchase applications fell 7% week over week and were down 18% year over year, per the Mortgage Bankers Association
UK inflation rose more than expected, increasing expectations of a Bank of England rate hike next month

A Tesla-SpaceX combination is described as likely by the guest, with SpaceX possibly funding AI ambitions through Tesla's robotaxi cash flow.

Safety claim of zero accidents over 3 million miles is presented as proof of superiority over human drivers without context on sample size or comparison data.
Speculative SpaceX merger likelihood described as 'likely' with no quantified probability; the guest admitted it is not certain and that shareholder votes are needed.

macro_points: Chase executives describe the U.S. small business economy as resilient, citing rising payrolls and consumer spending, while noting energy-driven inflation and geopolitical concerns.
A Chase survey reported small business owners are more optimistic about their own businesses (over 70% confident in one survey) than about the broader economy (about 30% in another cited survey).
A cited NFIB-style measure of U.S. small business optimism fell to a three-month low in September, with inflation, elevated borrowing costs, and energy prices weighing on sentiment.
Small businesses are described as about 40% of U.S. GDP and roughly two-thirds of new hires; these figures were stated by a Chase executive without a cited source.
Sunbelt population growth reportedly slowed in many states, with immigration policy, falling birth rates, and aging cited as factors.
Housing affordability is framed as a constraint on business growth and labor availability.

Unsourced statistics from Chase executives (e.g., small business share of GDP, new-hire share, Chase's own survey results) are presented without verification.
Market segments contain no risk discussion, but they are brief headline recaps rather than recommendations.

title: French Bond Risk Hits 15-Year High as Risk Gauge Climbs

findings.summary: A Bloomberg rates reporter discusses the sharp rise in French government bond risk, with the France-Germany yield spread reaching levels not seen since 2011. She attributes the move to a global bond selloff tied to an energy-price shock and ECB rate hikes, plus French fiscal and political concerns, notably the fragmented parliament and the 2027 presidential election. She notes spillover into Italian bonds and a rally in German bonds on French selloff days, and says the ECB has more tools than in the past. No specific stock or security is recommended.
macro_points: Global government bonds have sold off this year, with European bonds hit by an energy crisis.
The ECB has been forced into rate hikes, pushing euro-area yields higher.
The France-Germany yield spread has reached levels last seen in 2011.
French budget negotiations for next year are a key near-term catalyst; parliament is highly fragmented and governments have been toppled over budgets.
France's deficit is one of the largest in the euro area.
Presidential elections in 2027 are expected to bring a political shift investors cannot yet gauge.
Signs of contagion: Italian bonds move with France, while German bonds rally on days France sells off.
The ECB is watching fragmentation risk and has more tools than during the 2011-era euro debt crisis.
red_flags: Market-moving risk discussed without any stated positioning or specific trade recommendations, so there is little for a viewer to act on directly.
Transcript is auto-generated and some passages are unclear; figures are described qualitatively rather than with exact spread or yield numbers.

title: AI Is Tailwind, IBM CEO Says as Sales Rise

findings.summary: IBM reported third-quarter results that beat Street expectations on revenue ($17.1B vs ~$16.8B), software revenue ($7.8B vs ~$7.64B), operating EPS ($2.95 vs $2.86), and cash flow (~$3B). The CEO, in an interview, said the software slowdown seen in Q2 reversed in Q3, that growth is roughly flat for the year, and that he expects acceleration ahead, crediting AI tailwinds and a more constrained capex, partner-reliant strategy. A Bloomberg Intelligence analyst said the quarter was strong versus expectations, with software (Red Hat, Confluent) benefiting from AI-driven infrastructure upgrades, while consulting was a soft spot and services headcount trends were a concern.
macro_points: AI is expected to drive legacy infrastructure upgrades at existing enterprises, benefiting software.
Services and consulting firms (Accenture, TCS) still seeing sequential headcount growth, which the analyst finds surprising.
red_flags: Analyst's view that consulting was weaker than expectations and that legacy consulting projects are underperforming is only briefly addressed.
Claims of future acceleration come from the CEO and are not quantified in the video.
Price reaction or valuation not discussed; no risk discussion.

tickers.thesis: Q3 results beat expectations and the software slowdown reversed; the CEO expects acceleration, and the analyst sees AI driving upgrades in Red Hat and Confluent, though consulting is a drag.
